A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same visual-reasoning evaluation suite. Their complete text, figures, tables, and Appendices A–B are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original model and human evaluations, accuracy and F1 results, OCR controls, qualitative error analyses, and Circuit Connections regression results.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds newer-model results and a 75-trial decomposed Visual Scavenger Hunt experiment.

M1.justification: The three procedural task generators and their underlying operations remain unchanged. Revised transformation descriptions clarify the existing Object Re-Identification task. The guided scavenger-hunt experiment is an evaluation intervention, not a newly proposed model or algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Object Re-Identification with the same three variants, Visual Scavenger Hunt with chain lengths 2–4, and Circuit Connections with the same three coloring variants. The new decomposition experiment uses the existing chain-length-3 task and changes the testing procedure rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4 join the comparisons throughout Figures 2–6, and o3 expands from the main trials to additional variants. Conversely, o3 is removed from the F1 and regression comparisons because its secondary metrics were captured incorrectly, as disclosed in Appendix B.1.

E3.justification: Section 4.2 adds a distinct interactive evaluation over 75 trials: three sequential single-step queries pass each model answer into the next query. It reports full-sequence accuracy and final-step error conditioned on two correct preceding steps. This substantially extends the evaluation design to distinguish perception from autonomous chaining; it does not establish changes to the retained main protocols.

E4.justification: The new five-model decomposition study directly tests whether scavenger-hunt failures arise from individual perception steps or from chaining them. The appendix OCR-control table and its Qwen/Llama checks are removed, although the o4-mini OCR check remains in Section 4.2. Existing qualitative examples and distance/crossing analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions identify error bars as standard errors and report regression coefficients with p-values. Neither introduces repeated-seed reporting or a new uncertainty-estimation procedure. Changed whisker magnitudes and additional statistical result rows are result changes, not documented changes in statistical practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive newer-model and o3-variant results, plus guided-sequence accuracies of 90.67% for o4-mini and 88.00% for Gemini 2.5 in Table 1. These use a different procedure from the main task. Existing entries also change: o3's Standard re-identification accuracy goes from 55% to 54%, its secondary metrics are withdrawn, and Phi-4's Single Color crossing coefficient changes from -0.0004 to -0.000004. Reported error-bar magnitudes also change.

T1.justification: Section 4.2 introduces the conditional final-step error definition and a limited probability argument, using 0.94^3 to predict approximately 83% three-step success. No theorem or proof is added. The new Gestalt and attention-theory discussion supplies conceptual grounding rather than formal results.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains a three-part benchmark exposing nonlocal visual-reasoning weaknesses, now explicitly covering newer flagship models. The introduction narrows failure on at least one variant of every task to at least one variant of a task. The conclusion places greater emphasis on difficulty with tasks that resist natural-language reformulation.

C2.justification: v2 adds Gestalt/feature-binding explanations and interprets the decomposition experiment as identifying autonomous chaining as the stronger models' main bottleneck. For circuit tracing, v1 explicitly calls the strongest models inconclusive; v2 asserts that no model performs contour tracing and proposes choppy saccadic tracking, although later passages remain qualified. New limitations address synthetic-to-natural-image applicability and small evaluation samples.

D1.justification: v2 adds API identifiers and evaluation dates for new models, revises o3's dates, discloses its metric-capture bug, specifies the human evaluation sample size, and changes the repository destination to Princeton-VL. However, Appendix B loses the highest-reasoning setting, temperature 0.01, answer-normalization description, precise trial-size allocation, and statement that demonstrations were shared across models. These are substantial mixed changes in reproducibility information.

R1.justification: Related work shifts from re-identification, multiview consistency, and physical reasoning toward distinguishing primitive visual processing from Bongard/ARC-style abstract puzzles. Section 3 newly grounds the tasks in Wertheimer's Gestalt principles, Treisman and Gelade's feature-integration theory, and Ullman's visual routines. Several earlier references disappear, and the ChartQA reference is added.

P1.justification: Related Work, the Evaluation Design introduction, failure-mode discussions, and the conclusion undergo substantial paragraph-level rewriting. v2 adds a limitations paragraph, removes acknowledgments, reorganizes appendix subsections, and makes numerous terminology and grammar corrections. These changes extend beyond inserting new results.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redesigned and enlarged with revised examples. The performance plots are reformatted and expanded, a decomposition table replaces the removed OCR table in the document's table set, and Figure 10 uses a different example. Figure 11 changes from stacked to side-by-side panels. Figure 5 and the Object Re-Identification appendix images are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: Newer-model comparisons, the decomposition study, and explicit limitations improve breadth and diagnostic value. However, v2 removes important reproducibility settings and introduces stronger, inconsistent circuit interpretations: Section 4.3 describes most models as at or below chance across all variants despite Figure 6, and quotes Gemini's Unique Colors accuracy as 48% although the figure shows 52%. These reporting regressions and reduced caution offset meaningful additions, leaving the net quality change uncertain.
